At the edge of a small town, where the road gave up pretending to know where it was going, there was a mailbox with no house beside it.

It stood alone in a field of tall grass, painted blue once, though the weather had taken most of the color. Every morning, someone left a letter inside. Every evening, the letter was gone.

No one had ever seen the mail carrier.

Children dared one another to touch the mailbox. Teenagers wrote their secrets on folded notebook paper and slipped them through the narrow door. Old people, who had outlived nearly everyone they once knew, wrote long letters in careful handwriting and sealed them with lipstick, wax, or nothing at all.

The letters were never answered directly.

Instead, strange mercies began to appear.

A lost dog would return after three years. A storm would turn before reaching the valley. A woman grieving her brother would find, tucked into a library book, a photograph of them both laughing at a fairground decades earlier.

One winter, a boy named Elias wrote a letter that said only:

> I don’t know what I’m supposed to become.

He placed it in the blue mailbox and waited.

The next morning, there was no reply. There was only a small green shoot rising through the frozen ground beside the post.

Elias came back every day to look at it. By spring it had become a wildflower, yellow and bright, growing in a place where nothing should have survived.

Years later, Elias left town. He became a carpenter, then a father, then an old man with hands that always smelled faintly of cedar.

One autumn afternoon, he returned to the field.

The mailbox was still there. Smaller somehow. More rusted. The grass had grown around it like a tide.

He brought one final letter.

This time he knew what to write.

> Thank you for not telling me.

He slipped it inside, closed the little metal door, and stood quietly beneath the wide, patient sky.

That evening, as the sun lowered itself behind the hills, the mailbox’s faded blue paint caught the light and shone, just for a moment, as if it had never been touched by weather at all.
